meta.title: Who really said "Know thyself"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: “Know thyself” wasn’t coined by Socrates. It’s an ancient Delphic maxim inscribed at Apollo’s temple, traditionally credited to the Seven Sages.
meta.ogDescription: Not Socrates’ invention: “Know thyself” is a Delphic maxim carved at Apollo’s temple, older than Socrates and ascribed to the Seven Sages.

answer.label: Not Socrates — an ancient Delphic maxim
answer.authorName: The Delphic maxim (Seven Sages of Greece)
answer.authorDates: Inscribed at the Temple of Apollo, Delphi · attested by the 5th century BC
answer.sourceLine: “Know thyself” is one of the Delphic maxims carved in the forecourt of Apollo’s temple at Delphi, traditionally ascribed to the Seven Sages — Chilon of Sparta was most often credited, though ancient authors never agreed. Socrates repeatedly cited and probed it in Plato’s dialogues, which is why it clings to his name — but the maxim predates him and is not his coinage.

source.excerpt: γνῶθι σεαυτόν — “Know thyself.” One of three maxims (with “Nothing too much” and “Give a pledge and trouble is at hand”) displayed at the Temple of Apollo at Delphi.
trail: The phrase is one of the Delphic maxims inscribed at the Temple of Apollo, present by at least the 5th century BC — earlier than Socrates’ own lifetime.
Ancient tradition assigned it to the Seven Sages; Chilon of Sparta was most commonly named, but there was “no general agreement” among ancient authors.
Wikiquote records it as a Delphic maxim carved in the pronaos at Delphi, not as an original Socratic saying.
source.excerptNote: In Plato’s Protagoras, the Seven Sages are said to have jointly dedicated the maxim at Delphi; Socrates elsewhere treats it as the god’s own charge to examine oneself.

author.name: The Delphic maxims (Seven Sages of Greece)
author.heading: An inscription, not a Socratic coinage
author.metaLine: Inscribed at Delphi · attested by the 5th century BC · ascribed to the Seven Sages
author.bio: The Delphic maxims were a set of short ethical precepts displayed in the forecourt of the Temple of Apollo at Delphi, the seat of the Pythian oracle. Ancient tradition credited them to the legendary Seven Sages of Greece — Thales, Solon, Chilon and others of the 6th century BC — with Chilon of Sparta most often named for “Know thyself.” Modern scholars regard them as common proverbs that gained fresh authority from their prominent temple setting.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: Because Socrates made self-examination the heart of his philosophy and quotes the Delphic inscription in Plato’s dialogues, the two-word maxim is routinely pinned on him as if he coined it. He didn’t.

items.why: Socrates repeatedly invokes the Delphic “Know thyself” in Plato (Charmides, Phaedrus, Alcibiades I), but the maxim was already inscribed at Delphi and ascribed to the Seven Sages before him.

items.who: Chilon of Sparta / the Seven Sages
items.why: Chilon was the sage most often named as its author, but ancient sources disagreed; Plato’s Protagoras instead has the seven sages collectively dedicate it, and others attribute it to the oracle itself.

misattribution.truthLine: “Know thyself” is an anonymous ancient Delphic maxim older than Socrates — he popularized it, but did not write it.

context.heading: Why it sticks to Socrates
lead: Socrates turned self-knowledge into a method. In Plato’s dialogues he treats the Delphic “Know thyself” as a divine charge to examine one’s own soul rather than chase external things — so the maxim became inseparable from his legacy.

But the words were carved in stone at Delphi before Socrates philosophized in the Athenian agora. Attributing the phrase to him confuses the thinker who made it famous with the anonymous ancient tradition that produced it.
detailsBody: Three maxims were singled out at Delphi: “Know thyself,” “Nothing too much,” and “Give a pledge and trouble is at hand.”
Later writers piled up far longer lists of Delphic maxims, but these three are the ones consistently reported by ancient authors.
context.pull: He lived by it and argued about it — but he didn’t write it.
